explanation: A complex number extends the real number system by including the imaginary unit i (where i²=-1), written in the form a+bi, enabling solutions to equations with no real roots.
key_concepts: Standard form a+bi
Complex numbers as a superset of real numbers
Necessity for solving equations like x²+1=0

definitions.definition: A number of the form a+bi, where a and b are real numbers and i is the imaginary unit satisfying i²=-1.

worked_examples.problem: Identify the real and imaginary parts of 3+5i
Explain why x²+1=0 has no real solutions but does have complex solutions
steps: x²=-1 has no real solution (squares are never negative)
But x²=-1 gives x=±i in the complex system
worked_examples.answer: x = i or x = -i, using the definition i²=-1

practice_questions.q: Is 5 (with no i term) a complex number?
practice_questions.answer: Yes, it's 5+0i, a complex number with imaginary part 0
Yes, it's 0+3i, a purely imaginary number

exam_style_questions.q: Explain, using the quadratic formula, why x²-2x+5=0 has complex (non-real) solutions.
exam_style_questions.answer: Using the formula: x=[2±√(4-20)]/2=[2±√(-16)]/2; since the discriminant is negative, there's no real square root, requiring the imaginary unit: √(-16)=4i, giving x=1±2i

exam_style_questions.q: Solve x²+9=0 for x, expressing your answer using i.

common_mistakes: Forgetting complex numbers include all real numbers as a special case (with imaginary part 0)
Errors handling i² (must always simplify to -1, not left as i²)
Confusing purely imaginary numbers (like 3i) with complex numbers in general (which have both real and imaginary parts, though one can be zero)
tips: Every real number is technically also a complex number (with imaginary part 0) — real numbers are a subset of complex numbers
Always simplify i² to -1 wherever it appears in a calculation
Complex numbers exist specifically to give every polynomial equation a full set of roots, even when real solutions don't exist
summary: Complex numbers extend the real number system to give algebraic completeness — every quadratic (and higher) equation now has solutions, forming the essential foundation for this entire category.
quick_revision: z = a + bi, with i² = -1
Real numbers are complex numbers with imaginary part 0
Complex numbers solve equations with negative discriminants

explanation: Every complex number a+bi has a real part (a) and an imaginary part (b), both of which are themselves real numbers, used to classify and compare complex numbers.
key_concepts: Notation: Re(z) and Im(z)
Both parts are real numbers (the imaginary part is NOT bi, just b)
Equality of complex numbers requires matching both parts

definitions.definition: For z=a+bi, Re(z)=a, the real-number coefficient of the non-imaginary term.
For z=a+bi, Im(z)=b (not bi), the real-number coefficient of i.

formulas: z = a+bi: Re(z) = a, Im(z) = b

Find Re(z) and Im(z) for z=-4i

exam_style_questions.q: Given (2x-1)+(y+3)i = 7-2i, find x and y.
Explain why Im(z) is defined as a real number b (not bi), even though it's the coefficient of the imaginary term.
exam_style_questions.answer: Defining Im(z) as the real coefficient b (rather than bi) keeps the imaginary part as a purely real quantity, which is more useful for comparisons, equality conditions, and plotting on an Argand diagram (where Im(z) becomes the y-coordinate, a real number)

common_mistakes: Stating the imaginary part as 'bi' instead of just 'b' (a common and persistent notational error)
Errors solving for unknowns when equating complex numbers, forgetting to separately match both real and imaginary parts
Confusing Re(z) and Im(z) notation with the actual numerical value of z itself
tips: The imaginary part Im(z) is always a REAL number (just the coefficient b), never written with an i attached
When two complex numbers are equal, this gives you TWO separate equations: one for real parts, one for imaginary parts
Use this real/imaginary part equating technique to solve for unknown values within complex expressions
summary: Real and imaginary parts are the fundamental building blocks for classifying complex numbers, with the equality condition (matching both parts) being especially useful for solving equations.
quick_revision: Re(a+bi) = a; Im(a+bi) = b (not bi)
Two complex numbers are equal iff both real AND imaginary parts match
Real numbers: Im(z)=0; purely imaginary: Re(z)=0

explanation: The imaginary unit i is defined by the property i²=-1, forming the foundation for all complex number arithmetic and following a repeating cycle of powers.
key_concepts: Definition: i²=-1
Cyclical pattern of powers of i
Simplifying higher powers of i

definitions.definition: The number i, defined by the property i² = -1.

formulas: i¹=i, i²=-1, i³=-i, i⁴=1 (pattern repeats every 4 powers)

exam_style_questions.q: Simplify i²⁷, showing your method clearly.
exam_style_questions.answer: 27÷4=6 remainder 3; i²⁷=i²⁴×i³=(i⁴)⁶×i³=1×(-i)=-i

exam_style_questions.q: Simplify (2i)³, being careful to cube both the coefficient and i.

common_mistakes: Treating i as an ordinary variable and forgetting its special defining property (i²=-1)
Errors in the cyclical pattern, especially when finding remainders for high powers of i
Forgetting to cube/raise BOTH the coefficient and i when simplifying expressions like (2i)³
tips: Memorise the 4-cycle pattern: i¹=i, i²=-1, i³=-i, i⁴=1, then repeats — use the remainder when dividing the power by 4 to quickly simplify any power of i
When simplifying (ki)ⁿ, remember to raise BOTH k and i to the power n separately
Always simplify i² to -1 immediately wherever it appears in a calculation
summary: The imaginary unit's defining property and cyclical power pattern are essential computational tools used throughout every topic in the Complex Numbers category.
quick_revision: i² = -1 (the defining property)
Powers cycle every 4: i,-1,-i,1,...
Use remainder of (power ÷ 4) to quickly simplify any iⁿ

explanation: Complex numbers are added, subtracted, and multiplied using standard algebraic rules, treating i as a variable but always simplifying i² to -1 wherever it appears.
key_concepts: Addition/subtraction: combine real and imaginary parts separately
Multiplication: expand like binomials, then simplify i²=-1
Combining multiple operations in sequence

definitions.definition: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication of complex numbers, treating i algebraically but simplifying i²=-1.

exam_style_questions.q: Simplify (3+2i)² fully.
Find (1+i)³, showing full working.

Sign errors when subtracting complex numbers, especially with the imaginary parts
Treating i as if it were 1 or 0 in calculations rather than a genuine algebraic term
tips: Addition/subtraction: simply combine real parts together and imaginary parts together, exactly like combining like terms
Multiplication: expand fully as with any binomial product (FOIL method), then substitute i²=-1 and simplify
Always double-check that your final answer is in standard a+bi form, with i² fully simplified away
summary: Complex number arithmetic follows standard algebraic rules with one crucial extra step — simplifying i² to -1 — essential fluency for every subsequent Complex Numbers topic.
quick_revision: Add/subtract: combine real and imaginary parts separately
Multiply: expand like binomials, then substitute i²=-1
Always present final answer in standard a+bi form

explanation: The complex conjugate of a+bi is a-bi, obtained by flipping the sign of the imaginary part, with the key property that a complex number multiplied by its conjugate always gives a real (non-negative) result.
key_concepts: Definition: conjugate of a+bi is a-bi
z × z* is always real and non-negative
Used for rationalising complex fraction denominators

definitions.definition: For z=a+bi, the conjugate z* (or z̄) is a-bi.

formulas: z × z* = a² + b² (always real and non-negative)

steps: Flip the sign of the imaginary part

practice_questions.q: Find the conjugate of 5 (a real number)
practice_questions.answer: 5 (its own conjugate, since imaginary part is 0)

exam_style_questions.q: Given z=5-12i, find z* and verify that z×z* equals |z|² (which you should also calculate).
Prove that (z+z*) is always a real number, for any complex number z=a+bi.
exam_style_questions.answer: z+z*=(a+bi)+(a-bi)=2a, which is always a real number (twice the real part), since the imaginary parts exactly cancel

common_mistakes: Forgetting to flip the sign of the imaginary part correctly when finding a conjugate
Errors computing z×z*, particularly forgetting to simplify i² correctly
Confusing the conjugate with the negative of the complex number (z*≠-z in general)
tips: The conjugate simply flips the SIGN of the imaginary part — the real part stays exactly the same
z×z* always simplifies to a²+b², a purely real, non-negative number — this identity is extremely useful throughout the category
z* is NOT the same as -z: conjugate flips only the imaginary part's sign, while -z flips BOTH parts' signs
summary: Complex conjugates are a foundational tool, especially valuable for rationalising complex fractions and connecting directly to the modulus (via z×z*=|z|²).
quick_revision: z=a+bi ⟹ z*=a-bi
z × z* = a² + b² (always real, non-negative)
z* ≠ -z (different operations)

explanation: The modulus of a complex number is its distance from the origin on the Argand diagram, calculated using Pythagoras' Theorem on the real and imaginary parts.
key_concepts: Formula: |z|=√(a²+b²)
Geometric interpretation as distance from the origin
Relationship to the complex conjugate (z×z*=|z|²)

definitions.definition: For z=a+bi, |z| = √(a²+b²), representing the distance of z from the origin on the Argand diagram.

exam_style_questions.q: Given z=2+ki has modulus 2√5, find the possible values of k.
Find the modulus of (1+i)(2-i), first performing the multiplication.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to square each part before adding (using a and b directly instead of a² and b²)
Sign errors leading to unnecessary confusion (though squaring removes sign issues automatically)
Forgetting to take the final square root, leaving the answer as a²+b² instead
tips: This is exactly the same formula as vector magnitude and the coordinate distance formula — recognise this direct connection
Always take the positive square root — modulus (like distance) is never negative
Simplify surds in the final modulus wherever possible
summary: The modulus quantifies a complex number's 'size' as distance from the origin, directly paralleling vector magnitude and forming a key parameter in polar form representation.
quick_revision: |z| = √(a²+b²) for z=a+bi
Represents distance from the origin on the Argand diagram
Always a non-negative real number

explanation: The argument of a complex number is the angle its position vector makes with the positive real axis on the Argand diagram, typically measured in radians within the range -π to π (principal argument).
key_concepts: Argument as an angle, typically in radians
Principal argument range: -π < θ ≤ π
Using arctan with careful quadrant consideration

definitions.definition: For z=a+bi, arg(z) is the angle θ that the line from the origin to z makes with the positive real axis, typically in the range -π<θ≤π.

formulas: arg(z) = arctan(b/a), adjusted for the correct quadrant based on the signs of a and b

exam_style_questions.q: Find the argument of z=-3+4i, giving your answer in radians to 3 significant figures.
exam_style_questions.answer: Second quadrant; reference angle=arctan(4/3)≈0.927; arg(z)=π-0.927≈2.21 radians

exam_style_questions.q: Find the argument of z=2-2√3i, giving an exact answer.
exam_style_questions.answer: Fourth quadrant; reference angle=arctan(2√3/2)=arctan(√3)=π/3; since fourth quadrant, arg(z)=-π/3

common_mistakes: Using arctan(b/a) directly without adjusting for the correct quadrant, giving an answer outside the correct range
Confusing the reference angle (always acute, from arctan of the absolute values) with the final adjusted argument
Mixing degrees and radians inconsistently
tips: ALWAYS sketch the complex number's position on the Argand diagram first to identify which quadrant it's in, before calculating the argument
Calculate the reference angle using arctan(|b|/|a|), then adjust based on the quadrant: Q1 (as is), Q2 (π - ref), Q3 (-(π - ref) or ref - π), Q4 (-ref)
Confirm whether the problem expects degrees or radians, and stay consistent
summary: The argument captures a complex number's direction from the origin, requiring careful quadrant analysis — this is one of the most error-prone calculations in the entire category if rushed.
quick_revision: arg(z) = angle from positive real axis, range -π < θ ≤ π
Find reference angle via arctan(|b|/|a|), then adjust for quadrant
Always sketch the point first to confirm the correct quadrant

explanation: An Argand diagram plots complex numbers as points (or vectors) in a plane, with the horizontal axis representing the real part and the vertical axis representing the imaginary part.
key_concepts: Real axis (horizontal), imaginary axis (vertical)
Complex numbers as points or as position vectors
Geometric interpretation of addition, subtraction, and conjugation

definitions.definition: A coordinate plane used to represent complex numbers, with the real part plotted on the horizontal axis and the imaginary part on the vertical axis.

formulas: z = a+bi is plotted at the point (a, b)

worked_examples.problem: State the coordinates for plotting z=3-4i on an Argand diagram
steps: Real part is the x-coordinate, imaginary part is the y-coordinate

worked_examples.problem: Describe the geometric relationship between z and z* on an Argand diagram
steps: z*=a-bi has the same real part but opposite imaginary part
worked_examples.answer: z* is the reflection of z in the real (horizontal) axis

practice_questions.q: State the coordinates for plotting z=-2+5i
State the coordinates for plotting z=6 (a real number)
State the coordinates for plotting z=-3i
Describe the geometric effect of adding a real constant to a complex number, on the Argand diagram
practice_questions.answer: A horizontal translation (shift along the real axis)

practice_questions.q: Describe the geometric effect of multiplying a complex number by -1
practice_questions.answer: A 180° rotation about the origin (point reflects to the opposite quadrant)

exam_style_questions.q: Plot the points z₁=2+3i, z₂=-1+2i, and z₃=z₁+z₂ on an Argand diagram, and describe the geometric relationship illustrated (relating to vector addition).
exam_style_questions.answer: z₃=1+5i; plotting all three points, the relationship between z₁, z₂, and z₃=z₁+z₂ mirrors the triangle/parallelogram rule for vector addition, since complex number addition works identically to 2D vector addition when represented on the Argand diagram

exam_style_questions.q: Describe the locus of points representing z such that |z|=5 on an Argand diagram.
exam_style_questions.answer: This is a circle of radius 5 centred at the origin, since |z|=5 means every such point is exactly 5 units from the origin

common_mistakes: Reversing which axis represents the real part and which represents the imaginary part
Plotting points incorrectly, especially with negative real or imaginary parts
Not recognising the direct parallel between complex number operations and vector operations on the Argand diagram
tips: Real part is ALWAYS the horizontal (x) coordinate; imaginary part is ALWAYS the vertical (y) coordinate — this convention never changes
Complex number addition and subtraction behave exactly like 2D vector addition/subtraction on the Argand diagram — use this connection to build intuition
Many complex number properties (modulus, argument, conjugate) have direct, visualisable geometric meanings on this diagram
summary: The Argand diagram provides the essential visual foundation for this entire category, translating abstract complex number algebra into concrete, intuitive 2D geometry.
quick_revision: z=a+bi plotted at (a,b): real part=x-coord, imaginary part=y-coord
Addition/subtraction behaves like vector addition/subtraction
Conjugate = reflection in the real (horizontal) axis

images.description: An Argand diagram showing a complex number z=a+bi plotted as a point with its position vector drawn from the origin, labelled with the real axis (horizontal) and imaginary axis (vertical), the modulus |z| marked as the vector's length, and the argument θ marked as the angle from the positive real axis.
images.purpose: Establishes the fundamental visual framework for representing complex numbers, showing how modulus and argument relate geometrically to the real and imaginary parts.

explanation: Polar form expresses a complex number using its modulus and argument rather than its real and imaginary parts, written as r(cosθ+isinθ), useful for multiplication, division, and powers.
key_concepts: Conversion from Cartesian (a+bi) to polar r(cosθ+isinθ)
Conversion back from polar to Cartesian
Also written as r cis θ

definitions.definition: z = r(cosθ + isinθ), where r=|z| is the modulus and θ=arg(z) is the argument.

formulas: z = r(cosθ + isinθ), where r=√(a²+b²), θ=arg(z)

exam_style_questions.q: Convert z=-3-3i to polar form, giving the argument in radians to 3 significant figures.
exam_style_questions.answer: r=√(9+9)=√18=3√2; third quadrant, reference angle=arctan(1)=π/4, arg=-(π-π/4)=-3π/4 (or equivalently using the principal range); z=3√2(cos(-3π/4)+isin(-3π/4))

exam_style_questions.q: Given z=5(cos(2π/3)+isin(2π/3)), find the Cartesian form of z, giving exact values.

common_mistakes: Errors calculating the modulus or argument correctly before writing the polar form
Confusing the polar form's structure (cos first, then i sin) or forgetting the i inside the brackets
Sign or quadrant errors when finding the argument, propagating into an incorrect polar form
tips: Find r=|z| and θ=arg(z) carefully first (using previously covered techniques), then substitute directly into the polar form template
Always double-check the argument's quadrant using a quick sketch before finalising the polar form
Polar form is essential preparation for multiplication, division, and De Moivre's Theorem calculations covered next
summary: Polar form provides an alternative, often more powerful representation of complex numbers, particularly advantageous for multiplication, division, and finding powers/roots.
quick_revision: z = r(cosθ + isinθ)
r = |z| = √(a²+b²); θ = arg(z)
Convert back: a=r cosθ, b=r sinθ

explanation: Exponential form expresses a complex number as re^(iθ), using Euler's formula e^(iθ)=cosθ+isinθ, providing an elegant and compact alternative to polar form.
key_concepts: Euler's formula: e^(iθ)=cosθ+isinθ
Direct equivalence to polar form
Simplified notation for multiplication and powers

definitions.definition: z = re^(iθ), where r=|z| and θ=arg(z), based on Euler's formula e^(iθ)=cosθ+isinθ.

exam_style_questions.q: Using Euler's formula, show that e^(iπ)+1=0 (Euler's identity), and explain why this is considered a remarkable mathematical result.
exam_style_questions.answer: e^(iπ)=cos(π)+isin(π)=-1+0i=-1; so e^(iπ)+1=-1+1=0; this identity is remarkable because it elegantly connects five fundamental mathematical constants (e, i, π, 1, and 0) in a single simple equation

exam_style_questions.q: Find the exponential form of z=-4i, and verify by converting back to Cartesian form.
exam_style_questions.answer: r=4, θ=-π/2 (fourth quadrant boundary, pointing straight down); z=4e^(-iπ/2); verify: 4(cos(-π/2)+isin(-π/2))=4(0-i)=-4i ✓

common_mistakes: Confusing exponential form with polar form's explicit cos/sin notation (though they represent exactly the same mathematical content)
Errors in finding r and θ before constructing the exponential form
Not recognising exponential form when it appears in problems (e.g. multiplying two numbers in this form)
tips: Exponential form re^(iθ) is mathematically identical to polar form r(cosθ+isinθ) — Euler's formula is the bridge connecting them
This form is especially powerful for multiplication (add the exponents/arguments) and powers (apply standard exponent rules)
Euler's identity (e^(iπ)+1=0) is a famous, elegant special case worth knowing for its own sake
summary: Exponential form, based on Euler's remarkable formula, provides the most compact and algebraically powerful representation of complex numbers for multiplication and exponentiation.
quick_revision: z = re^(iθ) = r(cosθ+isinθ)
Euler's formula: e^(iθ) = cosθ + isinθ
Especially useful for multiplication and powers

explanation: Multiplying two complex numbers in polar form is remarkably simple: multiply their moduli and add their arguments, avoiding the more complex expansion needed in Cartesian form.
key_concepts: Multiply moduli, add arguments
Much simpler than Cartesian multiplication
Geometric interpretation: rotation and scaling

definitions.definition: For z₁=r₁(cosθ₁+isinθ₁) and z₂=r₂(cosθ₂+isinθ₂): z₁z₂ = r₁r₂[cos(θ₁+θ₂)+isin(θ₁+θ₂)].

practice_questions.q: State the general rule for multiplying complex numbers in polar form

practice_questions.answer: r(cosθ+isinθ)=z (unchanged, since multiplying by 1 with argument 0)

exam_style_questions.q: Given z₁=2(cos50°+isin50°) and z₂=5(cos(-20°)+isin(-20°)), find z₁z₂ in polar form, and convert to Cartesian form, giving exact or decimal values as appropriate.
Explain geometrically what multiplying a complex number by i does, using the polar multiplication rule (noting i has modulus 1 and argument π/2).
exam_style_questions.answer: Since i=1(cos(π/2)+isin(π/2)), multiplying any z by i multiplies its modulus by 1 (unchanged) and adds π/2 to its argument; geometrically, this is a 90° anticlockwise rotation about the origin, with no change in distance from the origin

common_mistakes: Attempting to multiply moduli and arguments together (rather than multiplying moduli and ADDING arguments — these are different operations)
Forgetting to combine the resulting argument correctly if it exceeds the standard range (adjusting by ±360° or ±2π as needed)
Confusing this simplified polar multiplication with the more complex Cartesian multiplication method
tips: Remember the pattern precisely: MULTIPLY the moduli, but ADD the arguments — mixing these up is a common and critical error
If the resulting argument falls outside the standard range, adjust by adding or subtracting 360° (or 2π radians) as needed
This multiplication rule reveals a beautiful geometric interpretation: multiplication by a complex number corresponds to a rotation (by its argument) combined with a scaling (by its modulus)
summary: Polar form multiplication is dramatically simpler than Cartesian multiplication, revealing the elegant geometric meaning of complex multiplication as combined rotation and scaling.
quick_revision: Multiply moduli: r₁×r₂
Add arguments: θ₁+θ₂
Geometric meaning: rotation + scaling

explanation: Dividing two complex numbers in polar form divides their moduli and subtracts their arguments, mirroring the elegant simplicity of polar multiplication.
key_concepts: Divide moduli, subtract arguments
Order matters for the argument subtraction
Geometric interpretation: rotation and scaling (reverse direction)

practice_questions.q: State the general rule for dividing complex numbers in polar form
practice_questions.answer: Divide moduli, subtract arguments (numerator's argument minus denominator's)

exam_style_questions.q: Given z₁=20(cos150°+isin150°) and z₂=4(cos80°+isin80°), find z₁/z₂ in polar form, then convert to Cartesian form.
exam_style_questions.answer: Moduli: 20/4=5; arguments: 150-80=70°; z₁/z₂=5(cos70°+isin70°); Cartesian: 5cos70°≈1.71, 5sin70°≈4.70; approximately 1.71+4.70i

exam_style_questions.q: Explain why the order of subtraction matters when dividing complex numbers in polar form, contrasting z₁/z₂ with z₂/z₁.
exam_style_questions.answer: z₁/z₂ has argument θ₁-θ₂, while z₂/z₁ has argument θ₂-θ₁=-(θ₁-θ₂); these are generally different values (unless θ₁=θ₂), and indeed z₂/z₁ is the reciprocal of z₁/z₂, confirming that division order genuinely matters, unlike with multiplication which is commutative

common_mistakes: Subtracting arguments in the wrong order (should be numerator's argument MINUS denominator's argument)
Dividing arguments instead of subtracting them (confusing the operation with the modulus rule)
Sign errors resulting in an argument outside the expected principal range
tips: Remember the precise pattern: DIVIDE the moduli, but SUBTRACT the arguments (numerator minus denominator) — this order matters, unlike multiplication
Always double check by considering: does z₁/z₂ make sense as 'undoing' some of z₂'s rotation and scaling from z₁?
This elegant division rule is the direct algebraic counterpart to polar multiplication, completing the toolkit for polar-form arithmetic
summary: Polar division mirrors polar multiplication's elegant simplicity, with careful attention to subtraction order (numerator minus denominator) being the key detail to master.
quick_revision: Divide moduli: r₁/r₂
Subtract arguments: θ₁-θ₂ (numerator minus denominator, order matters)
Geometric meaning: reverse rotation + scaling by ratio

explanation: Complex number equations are solved by treating i algebraically while applying the equality condition (matching real and imaginary parts separately) or standard algebraic techniques adapted for complex quantities.
key_concepts: Equating real and imaginary parts separately
Solving quadratics with complex coefficients or complex roots
Using conjugates to simplify equations

definitions.definition: An equation involving complex numbers, solved using algebraic techniques adapted to account for the imaginary unit i.

formulas: Equate real parts and imaginary parts separately to solve for unknowns

exam_style_questions.q: Solve the equation z²+2z+5=0 for z, using the quadratic formula and expressing your answer in a+bi form.
Find the values of a and b such that (a+bi)²=3+4i.
exam_style_questions.answer: a²-b²+2abi=3+4i; equate: a²-b²=3 and 2ab=4, so ab=2, b=2/a; substitute: a²-(2/a)²=3, a⁴-3a²-4=0; let u=a²: u²-3u-4=0, (u-4)(u+1)=0, u=4 (u=-1 rejected, a² can't be negative); a²=4, a=±2; if a=2, b=1; if a=-2, b=-1; so (a,b)=(2,1) or (-2,-1)

common_mistakes: Not separating and solving for real and imaginary parts as two distinct equations
Errors applying the quadratic formula when the discriminant is negative, requiring i notation
Forgetting complex solutions often come in conjugate pairs for equations with real coefficients
tips: When two complex expressions are set equal, this always gives TWO separate real equations (matching real parts, then matching imaginary parts) — solve both
The quadratic formula works identically for complex equations — a negative discriminant simply requires expressing the square root using i
For polynomial equations with REAL coefficients, complex roots always occur in conjugate pairs — use this as both a solving shortcut and a verification check
summary: Complex number equations extend familiar algebraic equation-solving techniques, with the equality condition (separately matching real and imaginary parts) as the essential new tool.
quick_revision: Equate real parts and imaginary parts separately
Quadratic formula works identically, using i for negative discriminants
Complex roots of real-coefficient equations come in conjugate pairs

explanation: Finding roots of complex numbers uses polar form and a generalised version of De Moivre's Theorem, producing multiple distinct roots evenly spaced around a circle on the Argand diagram.
key_concepts: nth roots produce n distinct solutions
Roots evenly spaced by 2π/n around a circle
Using polar form to systematically find all roots

definitions.term: nth root of a complex number
definitions.definition: A complex number w such that wⁿ=z, for a given complex number z; there are exactly n distinct such roots.

formulas: If z=r(cosθ+isinθ), the nth roots are: r^(1/n)[cos((θ+2πk)/n)+isin((θ+2πk)/n)], for k=0,1,...,n-1

worked_examples.problem: State how many distinct cube roots any non-zero complex number has
steps: The general rule for nth roots

practice_questions.q: How many distinct square roots does a non-zero complex number have?

Find the two square roots of -1 (matching known result)
Find the two square roots of 9

summary: Finding roots of complex numbers systematically generates n evenly-spaced solutions using polar form, building directly toward De Moivre's Theorem applications covered next.
quick_revision: nth roots: r^(1/n)[cos((θ+2πk)/n)+isin((θ+2πk)/n)], k=0,...,n-1
Always exactly n distinct roots, evenly spaced by 2π/n
Find ALL roots systematically, not just one

explanation: A complex locus is the set of points z satisfying a given condition (often involving modulus or argument), typically describing a circle, line, or ray on the Argand diagram.
key_concepts: |z-a|=r describes a circle centred at a with radius r
arg(z-a)=θ describes a ray from point a
|z-a|=|z-b| describes a perpendicular bisector

definitions.definition: The set of all points z on the Argand diagram satisfying a given equation or inequality involving z.

formulas: |z-a| = r: circle, centre a, radius r
|z-a| = |z-b|: perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a and b
arg(z-a) = θ: a ray from point a at angle θ

steps: This matches the circle formula directly
worked_examples.answer: A circle centred at (3,0) with radius 5

steps: This matches the perpendicular bisector formula, with points (0,2) and (4,0)
worked_examples.answer: The perpendicular bisector of the segment joining (0,2) and (4,0)

practice_questions.answer: Perpendicular bisector of the segment from (0,0) to (6,0), i.e. the vertical line x=3
A ray from the origin at 45° to the positive real axis

exam_style_questions.q: Sketch and describe the locus of points satisfying |z-3-4i|=5, and state whether the point z=6+8i lies on this locus.
exam_style_questions.answer: Circle centred at (3,4), radius 5; check (6,8): distance=√[(6-3)²+(8-4)²]=√(9+16)=√25=5; yes, this point lies exactly on the locus

exam_style_questions.q: Find the Cartesian equation of the locus |z-1|=|z-1-2i|, and describe the resulting line.
exam_style_questions.answer: This is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining (1,0) and (1,2); since both points have the same x-coordinate (1), the segment is vertical, so the perpendicular bisector is horizontal: y=1

common_mistakes: Confusing which point is the centre when reading |z-a|=r (remember it's centred at a, the value being subtracted from z)
Errors identifying the two points for a perpendicular bisector locus |z-a|=|z-b|
Sign errors when the locus involves subtraction of a complex number with negative real or imaginary parts
tips: |z-a|=r always describes a circle CENTRED AT a (read the value being subtracted directly as the centre) with RADIUS r
|z-a|=|z-b| describes points equidistant from a and b — this is always the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining these two points
Sketch the relevant points and loci on an Argand diagram to build strong geometric intuition for these relationships
summary: Complex loci translate algebraic conditions on z into elegant geometric shapes on the Argand diagram, connecting complex number algebra directly to coordinate geometry.
quick_revision: |z-a|=r: circle, centre a, radius r
|z-a|=|z-b|: perpendicular bisector of a and b
arg(z-a)=θ: ray from point a
